title: Blanche DuBois and the Reading Messiah that Wasn’t
author: Dr. Andy Johnson
summary: This is an excerpt from Andy Johnson's forthcoming book on the science of reading, arguing that teachers must be knowledgeable professionals and not direction-followers. He opens by admitting that in 1983 he simply followed the teacher's manual and that no one should treat any reading expert, himself included, as a messiah. Instead, he says teachers should listen to themselves, provided they have knowledge of the reading process, literacy learning, pedagogy and human development. Using Blanche DuBois's line about depending on the kindness of strangers, he warns that relying on publishers' scripted programs means handing decisions to profit-driven corporations that know nothing of the teacher's students or context. He claims publishers, legislators and ideologues alike want compliant automatons, but expects costly reading reforms to fail again as earlier ones did. The excerpt closes by stressing that mastery in teaching reading develops over time through knowledge, experience, conversation and reflection, and that reading instruction is never a settled science.
points: Johnson argues teachers should trust their own judgment, but only after building a real knowledge base about reading, literacy, pedagogy and development.
Scripted teacher's manuals mean decisions are made by strangers who do not know the teacher's students, context or situation.
He contends that corporate publishers are motivated by profit, so they will not change programs even when shown evidence that they are ineffective.
Publishers, legislators and ideologues are portrayed as wanting direction-followers instead of reading teachers who exercise professional judgment.
Becoming a master reading teacher is a lifelong process, and the excerpt insists the teaching of reading is never a settled science.
quotes: To make myself look better and sell more books, I could give you the impression that I always knew what I was doing when I was teaching reading in the classroom.
You should listen to you. However, the ‘you’ that you listen to should be a you-worth-listening-to. And for this, you need knowledge
Without a sufficient body of knowledge, you’re reliant on the directions that somebody else wrote.
The strangers who write directions for the teacher’s manuals don’t know you. They also don’t know your students, your context, or your teaching situation.
They want automatons. They want teachers to shut up and follow directions. They want direction-followers.
Becoming a master teacher is not a drive-through experience. It occurs over time with additional knowledge, experience, conversation, and reflection.
The one trait that all master reading teachers share is that they are never done learning. For a master teacher of reading, the teaching of reading is never a settled science.
